d: A legal wrong, crime (with which one is charged), misdeed, crime against God, a sin.

e.t: This word means “crime”—an offense or wrongful act that violates what is right. It names the wrongdoing itself rather than the person who commits it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Acts and Revelation, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding passages give each occurrence its particular setting. The word points to conduct that is treated as a real offense and therefore may be brought forward as something requiring judgment or acknowledgment.

d: To be ashamed, to be put to shame.
me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, first, Singular
Verb, peRfect, Active, Subjunctive, second, Plural
Verb, Present, Middle, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This word means “be ashamed”: to experience shame or feel disgraced. It expresses a person’s inward response when shame is present, rather than naming the cause of that shame. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, each in a different verse. The surrounding passage determines what produces the shame or how the feeling is being expressed in a particular sentence.

me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Subjunctive, second, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to consume” or “to destroy,” describing something being used up, devoured, or brought to ruin. It can express complete destruction rather than merely causing limited harm. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 9:54 and Galatians 5:15. Its exact force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the same: one thing consumes or destroys another until it is gone or seriously ruined.

me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, first, Singular
Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to repay”—to give back what is due in response to something received or done. It describes returning a fitting recompense, whether the result is favorable or unfavorable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages about God’s future judgment, repayment, and reward. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a fitting return for what has been received or done.

This word refers to an exchange or recompense—the return or repayment given in response to something received or done. It presents the idea of something being given back as a corresponding return, whether the exchange is favorable or unfavorable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, so its meaning is concentrated rather than broad. It is a noun describing the return itself, not primarily the action of exchanging. The surrounding passage determines what is exchanged and why the recompense matters in each occurrence.

d: A casting away, rejection, a loss.

e.t: This word refers to deprivation or rejection—the loss, removal, or refusal of something. It is a noun describing an outcome or condition rather than an action by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts and Romans, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains the experience of being deprived of something or being rejected. The related rendering “rejection” confirms this basic sense in one occurrence.

This word means “eager expectation,” expressing an intense, forward-looking anticipation of what is hoped for. It describes expectation marked by earnest desire rather than casual interest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 8:19 and Philippians 1:20. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its central idea remains a focused, eager anticipation directed toward an expected outcome.

This Greek New Testament word means “latrine,” referring to a place where human waste is deposited. It names a physical sanitary facility rather than a person, action, or spiritual quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 15:17 and Mark 7:19. In both passages, its basic sense is the destination to which bodily waste passes. The surrounding verse determines how that reference functions in the sentence, but the word itself has this concrete, ordinary meaning.

me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Vocative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to abhor”: to reject something with intense dislike or disgust. It describes a strong inner response rather than a mild preference or ordinary disagreement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Romans and once in Revelation. Its precise force in either passage is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a clear and emphatic refusal of what is detested.

d: To offer here and there, distribute, divide, hand over.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to distribute”—to give something out among people or assign it to them. It describes an action of dividing or sharing what is available rather than keeping it for oneself. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke, John, and Acts. Its use reaches across situations involving possessions or provisions, but the precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the purposeful giving or apportioning of something to others.

me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This word means “to be completely expended” or “to expend”—to use something up fully or to be spent entirely. It describes complete depletion rather than partial use. As a Greek New Testament word, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 12:15. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense centers on something being used up completely. The related active sense is “to expend,” emphasizing the act of spending or using fully.

This word means “eleventh,” identifying the person or thing in position eleven within an ordered sequence. It is an ordinal number term, not a general description of quantity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing twice in Matthew and once in Revelation. The word itself indicates sequence or rank, while the surrounding verse determines what group or order is being counted. Its exact references are Matthew 20:6, Matthew 20:9, and Revelation 21:20.

This word describes someone or something as honored—regarded with respect, esteem, or distinction. It can describe people who are publicly respected, as well as something presented as worthy of honor. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is clear but its particular force depends on the sentence where it appears. The central idea is honorable standing or recognized dignity, not merely outward appearance.

d: A rising up and out, resurrection.

e.t: This word means “resurrection”—the rising of the dead to life again. It names the event or reality of resurrection rather than describing a person, action, or feeling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the resurrection itself: life restored after death.

d: To stick fast, prop, fix firmly.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to immobilise” or “to stick fast.” It describes becoming firmly fixed so that movement is stopped or greatly hindered. As a verb, it expresses the action or result of something being held fast rather than remaining free to move. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:41, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: (used only of God), blessed (as entitled to receive blessing from man), worthy of praise.

e.t: This word means “praiseworthy” or “worthy of being praised.” It describes someone or something deserving honor and praise, especially when praise is directed to God. Its basic sense concerns the worthiness of the one being praised, rather than the act of praising itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, so it is an uncommon but repeated expression used across several books. The surrounding verse determines whom it describes and how the praise is expressed.

d: To make that which was dead to live, cause to live, quicken.

e.t: This word means “makes alive” or “to make alive.” It describes giving life, bringing something into living condition, or causing life to continue. In the New Testament, it is used of God’s life-giving power and of the raising or renewing of the dead and living. The wording may point to present life or future life depending on the sentence. It occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in John, Romans, and 1 Corinthians.

Joanan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 3:27, within the genealogy of Jesus. English Bibles render it as “Joanan” or “Joannan.” The available information identifies the person by name, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the name’s meaning. Its precise significance in Luke 3:27 therefore comes from the genealogy and its surrounding context.

d: Left behind; the rest, the remainder.

e.t: This word means “remaining”—what is left after others have been removed, departed, or otherwise no longer belong to the group being considered. It points to the remainder rather than the whole. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 15:17. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense is the people or things that remain. The word therefore draws attention to what is still present or left over.

d: A piece of landed property, a field; plural: possessions, property, possibly landed property, property in land.

e.t: This word refers to something a person owns—property, possessions, or wealth. It can describe material belongings held by an individual, whether considered generally as personal property or specifically as valuable goods. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in Matthew, Mark, and Acts. Its central sense remains the owned property itself, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on having such things, selling them, or holding them. The related meanings are “possession” and “wealth.”

This word means “bright” or “shining.” It describes something marked by light, brilliance, or a radiant appearance. Depending on the sentence, it can describe a person’s clothing, something visibly radiant, or a valued object whose brightness makes it attractive. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, appearing from Luke through Revelation. Its central idea remains brightness or shining, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is described.

d: Lucius, (a) of Cyrene, an early Christian, in the church of Antioch, by some identified with the evangelist Luke, (b) a Christian with Paul at Corinth, by some identified with (a).

e.t: Lucius is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, once in Acts 13:1 and once in Romans 16:21. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person identified by it; the surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which Lucius is intended in each passage. The English rendering preserves the name as “Lucius.”

This word means “corruption” or “defilement”—something that makes a person or thing morally or ceremonially impure. It describes the condition or influence of being polluted rather than naming a specific act by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:10. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is pollution or moral contamination.

d: Nicodemus, a member of the Sanhedrin.

e.t: Nicodemus is a personal name, referring to the man identified by that name in the Gospel of John. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a proper name used to identify one individual. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, all in John: three times in chapter 3, once in chapter 7, and once in chapter 19. The name is consistently rendered “Nicodemus,” so its meaning is chiefly its identifying function rather than a broader vocabulary concept.

d: In like manner, similarly, in the same way, equally.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: “Likewise” means in the same way, or similarly. It is an adverb that connects an action, condition, or statement with something already mentioned, showing that the same kind of thing applies again. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 30 times across 30 verses, so it serves as a recurring word for drawing a comparison or extending a preceding thought. Its exact force in any verse depends on what it connects, but its central idea remains correspondence: something happens or is true in a manner matching what came before.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to dig” or “to dig up,” describing the action of making a hole or removing earth. It is an action word used three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in two verses in Matthew and one in Mark. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: someone breaks into or moves through the ground by digging. The surrounding verse determines the particular object being dug and why the action is performed.

This word means “debt”: something owed by one person to another. It can describe an obligation that remains unpaid and therefore is due. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Matthew 6:12 and Romans 4:4. Its basic sense is the amount or obligation owed, while the surrounding verse determines how that idea is applied. The word’s meaning is therefore straightforward: a debt is something a person is responsible to pay or settle.

me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to keep on” or “to prolong.” It describes continuing something or allowing it to last longer, rather than ending it immediately. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 20:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the context, but its basic idea is extension or continuation. It functions as an action word describing something being continued or prolonged.

“Helmet” refers to protective headgear worn to guard the head. In the Greek New Testament, this noun occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “helmet.” The word names a concrete piece of defensive equipment rather than an action or quality. It appears in Ephesians 6:17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8; the precise force of each use belongs to its surrounding passage.

gl: to announce the gospel in advance
d: To preach the gospel beforehand, foretell good tidings.
me: Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This verb means “to announce the gospel in advance” or “to speak good news.” It describes proclaiming God’s good news beforehand, pointing to the message being announced before its fulfillment or wider reception. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 3:8. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact emphasis in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its central meaning remains the advance proclamation of good news.

This word refers to a woman who helps, supports, or acts as a patroness for others. It describes a person whose practical assistance benefits people in need, rather than merely naming someone who offers words of encouragement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 16:2, so its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains clear: a female helper or benefactor who gives support to others.

d: A hidden rock; fig: a flaw, stigma.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers either to a blemish—something marred or defective—or to a reef, a hidden hazard in the sea. These two meanings are distinct, so the surrounding wording determines which sense is intended. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Jude 1:12. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, its precise sense there cannot be stated more narrowly, but its basic meaning points to either a defect or a dangerous obstruction.

d: To take along as a companion.
me: Verb, second Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, second Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to take along with” someone. It describes bringing or accompanying another person as one goes, rather than simply going alone. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Acts and Galatians. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on who is being brought along and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains taking another person with you.

e.t: This word means “to be crucified with” or “to crucify with,” describing a person being put to death on a cross together with another person. It focuses on shared crucifixion rather than crucifixion viewed alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages describing people crucified alongside Jesus and figurative language about being crucified with him. Its exact force in each verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: A hole; the eye of a needle.

e.t: This word refers to an eye, and it can also describe a hole or opening. It is a noun naming a physical feature rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 19:24. The broader sense of an opening helps explain why the word can be rendered with either “eye” or “hole,” while its exact force in a passage depends on the surrounding context.

d: To puff up, make haughty; pass: to be puffed up, to be haughty.
me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, peRfect, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “be conceited”: to have an excessively high view of oneself. It describes a person whose thoughts and attitude are lifted up by self-importance rather than marked by humility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Paul’s letters to Timothy. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding sentence shows how that conceited attitude functions in context.

This word means “water” or “waters,” referring to the ordinary liquid itself. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for water as a real, recognizable substance, whether spoken of in the singular or as waters. The word occurs 76 times across 68 New Testament verses, so it is a broadly used everyday term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise significance in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To act the part, pretend; to answer, respond.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to pretend”: to act as though something is true or genuine when it is not. It describes a person presenting a false appearance rather than expressing what is truly in the heart. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 20:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the deliberate display of something unreal or insincere. The word therefore points to outward behavior that conceals a different inward reality.

This word means “hand,” referring to the physical part of the body used for touching, holding, working, washing, or acting. It can refer to one hand or to hands, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 177 times, so it is used broadly in ordinary descriptions as well as expressions involving human action or responsibility. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: the hand or hands, while the surrounding context determines the particular action or significance associated with them.

This word means “gall,” referring to a bitter substance. It is a noun used twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Acts. The word can identify a bitter material itself, while the surrounding sentence determines its particular use. In Matthew 27:34, it is connected with something offered to Jesus; in Acts 8:23, it appears in figurative language describing a person’s bitter condition. These references show the word’s ordinary sense of bitterness or a bitter substance, without requiring it to carry a broader meaning by itself.

This word describes someone who is gold-ringed or wearing a gold ring. It refers to a person identified by an ornament of gold, rather than naming the ring itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 2:2. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a person marked by wearing gold jewelry. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the person is treated there.

This word means “builder,” referring to someone who constructs or works on a building. It identifies a person by the work of building rather than by a spiritual quality, title, or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 4:11, so its normal meaning is established by this single use and the direct gloss “builder.” The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference is a person involved in building.
